properties.title: Red Creek Fir
properties.details:
Registry ID: 47
Species: coastal Douglas-fir (conifer)
Species rank: #1
Tree score: 784
Height 74 m · DBH 4.23 m · crown spread 23 m
Nearest town: Port Renfrew
Location: Red Creek
Ownership: Provincial land
Last measured: 5/1/1998
Site notes: It is one of largest known of its species and of the pine family. It is the only known tree on earth (except coast redwoods and giant sequoias) to be 7 feet thick, 144 feet off the ground.  The tree has a large, healthy crown, huge branches and a broken top. It is on a reserve.  Mid slope, toe mesoslope, aspect north.
Access notes: For excellent driving directions from Victoria BC, see https://www.ancientforestalliance.org/directions-red-creek-fir.php.   The tree is located off Red Creek Mainline and is accessed along a trail approximately 1/2 km from the road.  The trail head GPS is -124.22668 by 48.57998. The actual tree location is -124.220905 by 48.579422.

properties.title: Cheewhat Giant
properties.details:
Registry ID: 84
Species: western redcedar (conifer)
Species rank: #1
Tree score: 917
Height 55.5 m · DBH 5.84 m · crown spread 16 m
Nearest town: Youbou
Location: E Cheewhat L.
Ownership: Parks/reserves · Pacific Rim NP
Last measured: 5/1/1998
Site notes: In coastal rain forest, and in dense salal-huckleberry 30' high brush, about 1 km from a mainline road, and among many other very large cedars. Aspect west, slope 40-50%, upper mesoslope, convex.  

In 2006 the tree was observed to be very healthy with cambium intact for about 90% of the circumference - even the small scar where it is absent does not extend very far up the trunk. Above 40' the trunk breaks up into multiple stems.
Access notes: For good access directions to this tree, see "Vancouver Island Big Trees"  http://vancouverislandbigtrees.blogspot.ca/2010/06/directions-to-cheewhat-lake-cedar-trail.html.
The GPS co-ordinates for the trail head leading to tree #89 and #84 are 48.69273, -124.73593.

Site notes: This is beautiful healthy and straight tree is a "veteran" in a younger stand.  It is found growing deep in unlogged coastal rain forest valley. West southwest aspect, 5-10% slope, lower slope.  Tree Score was calculated using a hybrid approach.  It is based on the 1999 measurements of height and crown spread made by Van Pelt, and the 2020 measurement of diameter by TJ Watt. This approach was taken as the previous diameter estimate was found to be overestimated.  A full remeasure of this tree is planned and tree score will be recalculated.  The wood volume estimate of 266 cubic meters by R. VanPelt is based his diameter estimate of 4.07m.

properties.title: Joffre Giant
properties.details:
Registry ID: 141
Species: Engelmann spruce (conifer)
Species rank: #1
Tree score: 418
Height 38.8 m · DBH 2.27 m · crown spread 11.7 m
Nearest town: Mount Currie
Location: Joffre Creek
Ownership: Provincial land · Lil'wat Nation
Last measured: 10/31/2019
Site notes: This tree appears to be very healthy, some burls observed. Historic grown-over bole scars likely from boulders (slide). One fungi fruiting body located inside an old scar. No insect bore holes noted. Needles green and abundant to the tree top. Only one small cone located on ground, tree does not appear to be stressed. Tree dominated by Alder and surrounded by devils club, huckleberry, salmonberry, bracken fern, ribes and thimbleberry. (FG 2019) This tree is a perfectly formed sentinel with sprawling roots clinging to a huge boulder in the path of winter snow slides. The base swells to over 8 feet thick before expanding still further into massive, flaring roots.  ESE aspect, 40-45% slope, mid-slope, concave, (upper mesoslope, convex), avalanche deposition zone.  CWHds1, montane (RVP 1999)
Access notes: North of Joffre Creek. From Duffey Lake Rd. follow North Joffre Creek logging road for approx. 2.5 km. Cross creek and contour through forest to slide path. Tree is isolated in slide path/avalanche chute surrounded by slide alder. Tree visible from North Joffre logging road.

Last measured: 11/1/2021
Site notes: Healthy, has 6 reiterations (new leaders) and broken top at 115 feet, 5 leaders forming candelabra top.  Tree is at bottom of large avalanche chute.
Access notes: From the Lynn Headwaters Regional Provincial Park parking lot, take the Lynn Headwaters Trail toward Norvan Falls (7 km). Just before the falls, turn right onto the Coliseum Mountain trail. This trail is rugged and fairly vertical. Follow the yellow blazons and orange trail-marking tape. After about an hour, the trail levels out and is in more dense brush and old-growth. Follow the trail, crossing creek beds, until you reach a stony avalanche chute. You'll see Norvan Ponds (pools and waterfall) about 40 m to your left, down the chute. Keep walking on the path, which meanders up the stony avalanche chute. Look for the pink trail-marking tape in the bush to your right and walk about 15 m off the trail to the tree. The tree is above (to the right of) the path, below The Needles. The tree is not visible from the path.

Site notes: This tree is estimated to be in the 800-900 year range according to the local Haida. It is characterized by a very large trunk that diminishes little in circumference with height. Relatively healthy with broken top, CWHwh1. 
Diameter at branch appears to be about 2 m.
Access notes: Located within Gwaii Haanas National Park Reserve and Haida Heritage Site is the ancient village, and now current watchmen of Windy Bay, or Hlk'yah GaawGa. Windy Bay is on the western side of Lyell Island, and is home to a moderately sized salmon bearing stream and estuary.  From the watchmen cabin (south side of river), there is a well marked and maintained trail that follows the estuary up to the foot of the river, and crosses the river to the north side. From this point the trail winds into the woods, where you will walk for about ten minutes, before encountering the spruce tree right on the trail.

properties.title: Big Lonely Doug
properties.details:
Registry ID: 386
Species: coastal Douglas-fir (conifer)
Species rank: #3
Tree score: 701
Height 66 m · DBH 3.79 m · crown spread 18.3 m
Nearest town: Port Renfrew
Location: Gordon River V.
Ownership: Tree Farm Lic. · 46
Last measured: 4/18/2014
Site notes: The tree stands alone in a clearcut from 2012 and is hard to miss. It has a straight trunk, a broken top, and still has most of it's branches but did recently lose one of it's biggest in a wind storm. The hike into Big Lonely Doug is through difficult logging slash and should only be attempted by those with good balance.
Access notes: Driving Directions from Port Renfrew to Big Lonely Doug
1. km 0.0 - start at the Port Renfrew Community Center/Fire
Station and drive down Deering Rd 0.2 km
2. km 0.2 - continue over single lane bridge 1.1 km
3. km 1.4 - turn right at fork and continue for 1.4 km
4. km 2.7 - cross Deering Bridge and turn left onto the Gordon River Main (right goes to Lake Cowichan)
5. Stay on the mostly-paved Gordon River Main and after
approximately 5 km it will become gravel and you
will hit a Y where you go LEFT and cross a high bridge
over the beautiful Gordon River.
6. After crossing the bridge keep on the Gordon River Main
for about 1.5 km, staying to the RIGHT at the next Y.
7. Shortly after you will cross a small bridge over a creek
(Baird Creek). This is the Avatar Grove, the newly popular old-growth forest hiking area!
8. Continue past the Avatar Grove on the Gordon River Main
for approximately 4.5 km and take your FIRST RIGHT onto
Edinburgh Main road. (Note: its a smaller looking road)
9. You will soon cross over a bridge above a very tall canyon
on the Gordon River. *Note: From here on 4x4 vehicles with
good clearance are recommended!
10. Follow the rough road as it veers uphill and then right. Continue
on the main road for approximately 5 minutes.
11. A giant clearcut from 2012 will appear on your right hand
side. In that clearcut you will see two big Douglas-firs left
standing - the second one is Big Lonely Doug.
*NOTE: The hike into Big Lonely Doug is through a difficult
clearcut and should ONLY be attempted by those with good
balance.

Site notes: Fairly healthy.  Appears to have a broken top at about 8" diameter (guess).  Small stand of very large trees in the shallow valley of Finlay Creek.  Devil's Club.  This tree is within 20 feet of the creek.  Area logged to within a few hundred meters about 100 years ago.  A new logging road (Finlay FSR) was constructed about 200 meters south of the tree.
Access notes: From Peachland take Princeton Ave. to McDougald Rd. which turns into Munro Lake FSR.  Follow Munro FSR for 6.7km and turn left onto the new Finlay FSR. There is a wide spot for parking on the new Finlay FSR at the 7Km sign.  Park there and walk ahead to Finlay Creek.  Hike up the creek a few hundred meters to the tree.  An access map is available (see the "Tree images and location maps" tab). 
PLEASE NOTE: The Munro FSR reconstruction project is mostly complete.  The road is much improved but will still be muddy in spots.  Note that it is a ONE LANE ROAD with pull-outs.  During active logging you must be prepared to back up to a wide spot in the road if you meet a truck.

Nearest town: Cranbrook
Location: Standard Hills
Ownership: Provincial land · Cranbrook Comm. For.
Last measured: 6/25/2015
Site notes: Rock face to west, growing on slope [~20],  trunk slants ~20 to northeast, several large branches, trunk concave to northeast [old fire scar?], cross-section of trunk is not circular - estimate 22" x 27" diameter.
Access notes: Cranbrook Community Forest. From Cranbrook, take Highway 3/95 northeast about 12 km to Mission/Ft. Steele Road. Turn left and follow this road towards the rifle range. At about 0.4 km turn left on an old logging road and follow it southwest and west about 2.3 km, where it turns south and then continues west, passing three ponds to the south of the road. The third of these ponds is called Double Duck Lake. Continue past it for about 500 m. There is a meadow on the south side of the road with a big tree at the midpoint of its edge along the road. Park. Hike northeast up a gully between two hills about 600 m to the big juniper, which is growing at the base of a rock face on the west side of the gully. Alternatively, from Double Duck Lake, hike due north and follow a ridge about 500 m. Turn west and walk down into a gully, where the juniper grows at the base of that east-facing rock face.

Ownership: Parks/reserves · Carmanah Walbran PP
Last measured: 7/14/2016
Site notes: Smooth mossy trunk without much buttressing. Situated on a low riparian terrace.
This tree was one of ten nominated by a UBC research team in the Carmanah Valley in July 2016. The team consisted of Matthew Beatty, Jon Degner, Vincent Hanlon, James Luce, and Ryan Murphy, as well as Sally Aitken, James Frystak, and TJ Watt, who were present part of the time.
Access notes: From the Carmanah PP parking lot, hike down the valley mist trail to the first junction. Turn left, towards the Three Sisters. A few minutes of walking, past a gully containing an eighty-meter giant, leads to low riparian terrace. Gatekeeper is on the right side of the trail (facing upstream) at the bottom of a staircase which is the second descending staircase after the junction.

This tree was one of ten nominated by a UBC research team in the Carmanah Valley in July 2016. The team consisted of Matthew Beatty, Jon Degner, Vincent Hanlon, James Luce, and Ryan Murphy, as well as Sally Aitken, James Frystak, and TJ Watt, who were present part of the time.
Access notes: From the Carmanah Walbran PP main trailhead, hike down the Valley Mist trail to the junction. Turn left towards the three sisters, and continue until you reach the creek. The stand of trees containing the Diver is just past a small wooden bridge over a dry creekbed. After the bridge there is a washout, and the trail divides in two, with a bypass around the washout. Facing upstream where the bypass rejoins the main trail, the Diver is on the side of the trail to the left. Carmanah Creek is visible from it's base. It is the most upstream (north-easterly) of the stand in which it is situated.

Access notes: From the Carmanah Walbran parking lot (access from Rosander Main), follow signs for the Valley Mist trail. properties.title: Alberni Giant 1513-002
properties.details:
Registry ID: 453
Species: coastal Douglas-fir (conifer)
Species rank: #4
Tree score: 683
Height 65 m · DBH 3.64 m · crown spread 24.1 m
Nearest town: Port Alberni
Location: Riverside Main
Ownership: Provincial land · BCTS Legacy Tree
Last measured: 10/17/2019
Site notes: 1513-002 is a Douglas-fir in good health. There are no apparent signs of rot present upon a visual inspection of the tree. The tree is largely intact with only a few small broken limbs present in the upper portion of the canopy. there are several moderate-sized burls (approximately 1m across and flattened) on the up-slope side of the tree. It is located within the CWH vm1 and is situated on a small bench located on the lower slope with a NE aspect. The tree can be considered to be windfirm as it is sheltered within a 12.1 hectare Old Growth Management Area. This OGMA contains several other Legacy Trees (two Western Redcedar; 1513-001 and 1513-003).There is minimal evidence of historic windthrow in the vicinity of 1513-002 or throughout the OGMA.
Access notes: Follow Hiway 4 west through Port Alberni. After crossing the 'Orange' bridge over the Somass River, drive 0.6km and then turn left on to McCoy Lake Road. Follow McCoy Lake Road to the junction with Stirling Arm Drive. Follow Stirling Arm Drive to the intersection with Ash Main. Turn left onto Ash Main and drive 1km to the junction with Stirling Main. turn right onto Stirling Main and follow it for 12km to the junction with Gracie Main. Turn left onto Gracie Main and follow it for 6km to the junction with Gracie Hook-up. Keep right onto the Gracie Hook-up and follow it for 2km to the junction with Nahmint Main. Turn right onto Nahmint Main and drive 1.2km to the bridge crossing the Nahmint River. Once across the one-lane bridge, drive 0.2km to the junction with Riverside Main. Turn left onto Riverside Main and drive 1.7km to Block 1513 located on the west side of the road. If you drive past a small weedy lake to your right, you have driven past Block 1513 and the tree. There is a small road on your right just past the lake which makes a convenient turnaround. The tree is very visible along the skyline beyond the southern boundary of Block 1513. There is a rough trail from the road (approximately 20m past the southern falling boundary of the block that leads up to 1513-002. You will pass a large Western Redcedar (Legacy Tree 1513-001, 3.15m in diameter or 9.9m in circumference) as you climb the slope up to 1513-002. There is another large Western Redcedar (Legacy Tree 1513-003, 3.11m in diameter or 9.8m in circumference) located approximately 25m up slope of 1513-002. All trees are marked with bright yellow BCTS Legacy Tree plaques. Use caution when traveling on gravel Forest Service roads. These are active industrial roads and expect to meet large vehicles at any time!

properties.title: yellow-cedar · Registry 454
properties.details:
Registry ID: 454
Species: yellow-cedar (conifer)
Species rank: #29
Tree score: 377
Height 37 m · DBH 2.01 m · crown spread 9 m
Nearest town: Macoah
Location: Kite Lake
Ownership: Provincial land · BCTS Legacy Tree
Last measured: 7/24/2018
Site notes: C4DT-001 is located in CWHvm2(09) on a steep (60%) mid-slope with a northeast aspect. The tree is growing on a small rocky knoll surrounded by medium colluvium.
Access notes: Take Hiway 4 west from Port Alberni. Drive approximately 80km to the Maggie Lake FSR. Turn left and follow Maggie FSR for 11km to Macoah Villagfe turn-off. Keep left on Maggie FSR and drive another 4km to the end of Maggie FSR. Keep left and you are now on Toquaht FSR. Drive 9km to the junction with Lucky FSR. Turn right onto Lucky FSR and drive 2.5km to the junction with Black Peaks FSR. Keep left and follow Lucky FSR for another 2.4km. You will pass two lakes on your right. The second (and larger lake is Kite Lake). Once past Kite Lake, you will come to a major junction. Keep right and continue along Lucky FSR for another 1.4km. there will be a deactivated and brushed in spur road on your right. This is the start of teh rough trail up to Block F004C4DT. Hike up the spur for 700m to a very overgorwn junction. Keep to the left and hike a further 450 m. You will come across some yellow flagging that indicates a rough trail up to F004C4DT. Nearest town: Kimberley

Ownership: Provincial land · CanFor
Last measured: 11/4/2019
Site notes: Minimal lower stem damage/decay, but displays signs of larger branch and top breakage characteristic of larger larches. The largest larch was located at the toe of a scree slope, NW aspect.  Growing all around the edges scree slope were similarly large larches: 26 trees measured were >3m and 4 were >4m. Many of the trees, especially those on the southeast (top of the slope) side of the scree slope bore fire scars and charring suggestive that they survived a fire decades ago.  Height to live crown 8m, ht to broken top 39m, branches ascend upward a few meters. Woodpecker holes on bottom 2 m.
Access notes: From Kimberley : Take Hwy 95A towards Cranbrook. Turn R onto St Mary's Lake Rd. Turn L onto Lakeside Rd and continue onto Hellroaring FSR. Keep R at first fork, then stay L on Hellroaring FSR (do NOT go onto Meachen FSR). You will cross Hellroaring Creek over a bridge.TThe tree is 50m back from the 9km marker and roughly 4km past the 31km marker. The boulderfield will be on your L, the last km marker I remember seeing was for 30km up. If you cross a 2nd bridge, you have gone too far (but there is a good turnaround spot there). The biggest larch is within 20m of the road. The others can be located by scrambling around the boulderfield. 
From Cranbrook: Take Hwy 95A towards Kimberley. Continue through Marysville. Turn L onto St Mary's Lake Rd; the rest is the same as above.

properties.title: Ponderosa pine · Registry 544
properties.details:
Registry ID: 544
Species: Ponderosa pine (conifer)
Species rank: #7
Tree score: 341
Height 45.9 m · DBH 1.45 m · crown spread 14.7 m
Nearest town: Naramata
Location: Three Blind Mice
Ownership: Provincial land · Okanagan Forest
Last measured: 4/18/2020
Site notes: The tree is located at the base of a moderate west facing slope in a relatively flat area.  The tree is in good health and does not appear to have a broken top.  A good view of the top of the tree is difficult due to the surrounding Ponderosa pine and Douglas-fir trees, which partially block the view. The area is used by mountain bike and hiking enthusiasts.  In general, the area is characterized by steep rocky bluffs and flat benches.  The larger trees tend to grow on the benches or in ravines where moisture is more plentiful.  The area is used by whitetail deer, elk, black bear and coyote, as well as numerous species of birds.
Access notes: The Three Blind Mice trail network can be accessed by driving from Penticton north along Naramata Road.  Turn right (about 6 to 7 km from downtown Penticton) onto Riddle Road and drive to the top of the road where roadside parking is available.  The walk or ride to the tree is about 5 to 5.5 km one way.  Enter the attached URL into your browser to access the trail map:  look for the intersection of Pinecone and Ponderosa trails, located near the middle of the trail network.  https://www.trailforks.com/region/three-blind-mice/map/?activitytype=1&z=12.0&lat=49.56396&lon=-119.55505

properties.title: Chek Narrows Giant
properties.details:
Registry ID: 545
Species: coastal Douglas-fir (conifer)
Species rank: #118
Tree score: 442
Height 48.1 m · DBH 2.23 m · crown spread 12.8 m
Nearest town: Squamish
Location: Chek Canyon Rec. Site
Ownership: Provincial land
Last measured: 10/4/2020
Site notes: Visibility of crown is limited. But top is dead (at least several meters in height) and broken. Top is >40cm where broken.  The tree is located on flattish ground next to a small creek in the base of a deep canyon. The tree is the
largest so far discovered in an area of undisturbed old growth which is approximately 700m long and extends for several
hundred metres up both side of the canyon. In the area there are approximately one hundred firs of one meter diameter or
bigger and at least five trees around two meter diameter. I believe the area has never been logged due to very large talus
boulders and other physical barriers created by the canyon topography.
Access notes: From Squamish (junction of Cleveland avenue and Highway 99) drive 24.5 km north on Highway 99 to the Conroy Creek FSR
entrance.
- Drive about 500m up the FSR to a large parking area and campground. This is the Chek Canyon rec site.
- A climbers' access trail leads horizontally south from here. Hike this trail for about 5 mnutes until its end at a cluster of very
large talus boulders under steep cliffs equipped for rock climbing.
- continue bushwhacking south for about 600m along the base of the canyon. Progress is difficult because of numerous fallen
trees, the creek and talus/ scree slopes.

properties.title: Bumblebee
properties.details:
Registry ID: 547
Species: coastal Douglas-fir (conifer)
Species rank: #18
Tree score: 621
Height 66.8 m · DBH 3.12 m · crown spread 19.1 m
Nearest town: Whyac
Location: E. Fork, Klanawa
Ownership: Tree Farm Lic. · 44
Last measured: 4/22/2020
Site notes: CWHvh1 07.  The top of the crown is bare and the canopy has classic spiralling form. On the uphill side of the tree the trunk has large columnar veins and a distinctive scar bare of bark (Approx. AM525 x 0.75m). Bumblebee stands at a lower slope position, at the edge of cut-block along a small and steep drainage populated by western redcedar.  The Bumblebee Tree stands on a cutblock above the Hummingbird Spruce Grove. For more detailed information about the trees of this region visit
the Vancouver Island Prominent Tree Survey, a project hosted by the coastaltrailcollective.com.
Access notes: From the small town of Youbou, on the Eastern end of Lake Cowichan, head Westward on the North Shore Road,
continuing all the way past the lake on Cowichan Main and eventually following the Nitinat River.
Turn right at T-Intersection ( 48.8627379, -124.6438995 ) over the bridge which crosses Nitinat River, following
Carmanah Main. A visit to the waterfalls on the Little Nitinat Falls is recommended for a quick break (unmarked pull
off near 48.871476, -124.687404 ).
Follow Carmanah Main until a bridge on your left crosses the Little Nitinat River onto Flora Main ( 48.8994754,
-124.6887141 ).
Follow Flora until you reach Upper Klanawa Main ( 48.861963, -124.739748 ) and turn left.
Not long after passing Newstead Main (do not take this road), the road starts climbing and splits. Take the left spur
K-265, up a steep pitch and around a tight bend ( 48.8267934, -124.7812745 ). After some time, along the South side
of K-265 there are a couple of small lakes accessed via a short spur (approx 48.8274633, -1248130282 ), where one
can visit the Fairy Bell Cedar at Dorothy Lake (at the head of the second lake, 48.825688, -124.822826 ).
Coming to another T-Intersection ( 48.8307925, -124.8372049 ), turn left and continue straight past another
intersection and follow it until you reach the spruce flats and recently logged areas at the bottom of the valley (approx
48.7969942, -124.8668236 ). This is where the Main and East Forks of the Klanawa River meet. This new road
bends East and becomes very coarse. It is advised that one parks in a safe location and walks to the Bumblebee
Tree from the road (starting at 48.801119, -124.832387 ).
*Alternatively the Hummingbird and adjacent forest stands can be reached by crossing one of the numerous log-jams
on the Klanawa River East Fork. Park on Newstead Main , and find a log-jam that you can cross safely ( 48.799488,
-124.817626 ) or ( 48.802287, -124.808875 ) for example. Be sensible, do not attempt when the river is flowing high,
and no I am not responsible if your shoe soles are slippery and your iphone goes for a swim ;) Keep your electronics
safe in a ziplock or wet bag. Personally, we prefer using Newstead Main, the road is in better condition and it is a
more straightforward route.
Please be advised that this is an ACTIVE logging area, follow suitably safe driving techniques and be vigilant and
courteous to other road users. It is advised to only visit this area on weekends when logging activities are minimal.
This is a remote area without cellular reception so plan your trip accordingly. Input your coordinates before you leave
home. In general the gravel road driving is reasonable for most vehicles, but fill your tank and definitely bring a full
sized spare tire along for this trip.

properties.title: 3PP
properties.details:
Registry ID: 551
Species: coastal Douglas-fir (conifer)
Species rank: #26
Tree score: 612
Height 68 m · DBH 3.03 m · crown spread 18 m
Nearest town: Youbou
Location: Nitinat R. - Macoola
Ownership: Tree Farm Lic. · 44
Last measured: 6/24/2019
Site notes: Gradually tapering and with a distinctive burl, the trunk splits into two healthy looking upward facing
leaders at approximately the 40m mark.
Located on a flat and sandy riparian floodplain, 3PP is a fine Douglas fir standing amidst Bigleaf
Maple, Hemlock and Sitka spruce about 60m from the bank of the Nitinat River.
This floodplain is part of a series of high quality, intact riverside patches of old growth standing
between the Eastern and Western portions of the Nitinat River Ecological Reserves. Sitka Spruce begin to
Reach full potential in the floodplains and Douglas fir become less abundant at river level. Here and across
the river in Macoola Grove, one will find the Red Listed Tooth- leaved Monkey flowers and Blue Listed
Scoulers corydalis carpeting the floor during the late spring and summer.
For more detailed information about the trees of the Central Nitinat River and the Macoola Grove region
visit the Vancouver Island Prominent Tree Survey, a project hosted by the coastaltrailcollective.com
Access notes: From the small town of Youbou, head Westward on the North Shore Road, following along the shore of Cowichan
Lake. Arrive at a signposted split between Bamfield and Nitinat and head left towards Nitinat. Driving past the head
of the Lake, you eventually enter the Nitinat River Valley. At the entrance of Nitinat River Ecological Preserve
(Eastern Portion 48.901189, -124.545689 ) you will encounter old-growth Douglas fir forest and some roadside
CMTs. Have a look at the impressive Nitinat Fir (just below the road, 48.893787, -124.556285 ).
It is also worth checking out the canyon section of the Nitinat river ( 48.895723, -124.558131 ).
A couple of hundred meters past the turnoff for Granite Main, find a safe place to park. On foot, follow an old spur on
the north side of the road ( 48.876268, -124.587473 ) briefly. When the spur becomes overgrown, head left
( 48.878611, -124.585422 ) through the bush. Heading slightly downhill, start contouring to your right along the hillside
until you encounter an impressive stand of Fir and Hemlock on the slope above the river. Here you will encounter the
Cauliflower Mushroom Fir. Follow the lower slope around a corner (northward and upstream) for 50m or so, staying
above the dense brush along the river edge. Once you can easily cross onto the river flats, find your way to the river
edge and safely fjord across the river, just above the bend. You should be able to see a large spruce and you may be
able to see 3PPs double leaders a little further back from the shore. The tree is located on the flats about 60m from
shore amongst sword ferns.
Please be advised that this is an ACTIVE logging area, follow suitably safe driving techniques and be vigilant and
courteous to other road users. It is advised to only visit this area on weekends when logging activities are minimal.
This is a remote region without cellular reception so plan your trip accordingly. Input your coordinates before you
leave home. In general the gravel road driving is reasonable for most vehicles, but fill your tank and definitely bring a
full sized spare tire along for this trip. There are some basic amenities available in the Village of Nitinat. Only cross
the river when the flow is low, it is recommended to have your electronics in watertight bags and please be careful.
properties.access_notes:
From the small town of Youbou, head Westward on the North Shore Road, following along the shore of Cowichan
Lake. Arrive at a signposted split between Bamfield and Nitinat and head left towards Nitinat. Driving past the head
of the Lake, you eventually enter the Nitinat River Valley. At the entrance of Nitinat River Ecological Preserve
(Eastern Portion 48.901189, -124.545689 ) you will encounter old-growth Douglas fir forest and some roadside
CMTs. Have a look at the impressive Nitinat Fir (just below the road, 48.893787, -124.556285 ).
It is also worth checking out the canyon section of the Nitinat river ( 48.895723, -124.558131 ).
A couple of hundred meters past the turnoff for Granite Main, find a safe place to park. On foot, follow an old spur on
the north side of the road ( 48.876268, -124.587473 ) briefly. When the spur becomes overgrown, head left
( 48.878611, -124.585422 ) through the bush. Heading slightly downhill, start contouring to your right along the hillside
until you encounter an impressive stand of Fir and Hemlock on the slope above the river. Here you will encounter the
Cauliflower Mushroom Fir. Follow the lower slope around a corner (northward and upstream) for 50m or so, staying
above the dense brush along the river edge. Once you can easily cross onto the river flats, find your way to the river
edge and safely fjord across the river, just above the bend. You should be able to see a large spruce and you may be
able to see 3PPs double leaders a little further back from the shore. The tree is located on the flats about 60m from
shore amongst sword ferns.
Please be advised that this is an ACTIVE logging area, follow suitably safe driving techniques and be vigilant and
courteous to other road users. It is advised to only visit this area on weekends when logging activities are minimal.
This is a remote region without cellular reception so plan your trip accordingly. Input your coordinates before you
leave home. In general the gravel road driving is reasonable for most vehicles, but fill your tank and definitely bring a
full sized spare tire along for this trip. There are some basic amenities available in the Village of Nitinat. Only cross
the river when the flow is low, it is recommended to have your electronics in watertight bags and please be careful.
properties.site_notes:
Gradually tapering and with a distinctive burl, the trunk splits into two healthy looking upward facing
leaders at approximately the 40m mark.
Located on a flat and sandy riparian floodplain, 3PP is a fine Douglas fir standing amidst Bigleaf
Maple, Hemlock and Sitka spruce about 60m from the bank of the Nitinat River.
This floodplain is part of a series of high quality, intact riverside patches of old growth standing
between the Eastern and Western portions of the Nitinat River Ecological Reserves. Sitka Spruce begin to
Reach full potential in the floodplains and Douglas fir become less abundant at river level. Here and across
the river in Macoola Grove, one will find the Red Listed Tooth- leaved Monkey flowers and Blue Listed
Scoulers corydalis carpeting the floor during the late spring and summer.
For more detailed information about the trees of the Central Nitinat River and the Macoola Grove region
visit the Vancouver Island Prominent Tree Survey, a project hosted by the coastaltrailcollective.com

properties.details:
Registry ID: 555
Species: western larch (conifer)
Species rank: #2
Tree score: 377
Height 54 m · DBH 1.52 m · crown spread 14 m
Nearest town: Fernie
Location: Snakebite Trail
Ownership: Provincial land · Fernie Alpine Resort
Last measured: 6/29/2020
Site notes: Many fire survived veteran Western Larch spire up from the Western Red Cedar forest on the lower slopes of the Lizard Range. The difficulty field locating them, in the absence of a trail, is the thick alder, buckbrush, and devil's club choked underbrush that presents the challenge. The larch tree sampled was right beside the Snakebite Mountain Bike Trail, so can be located a bit more easily.
This stand of trees appears very healthy, likely, with todays fire suppression prioratization in proximity to an urban area, could live another 500 years? Age estimate from annular ring count of a "cookie" of a similar diameter tree in close proximity is 425 years.
Access notes: To locate this site on the Lizard Range, drive right on through the campsite on Mount Fernie Park Road, until you reach a trailhead kiosk on the left, where an obvious aluminum bridge crosses Lizard Creek. Immediately after exiting from the bridge turn left onto the signed Gorby Trail. This is actually an old road that leads up into the lower basin of Cedar Bowl. Upon arrival in the big basin, take the road to right, Red Tree Road, and follow it for about 500 m. where the Snakebite Trail ushers you into the forest on your right.

properties.title: Stumble On
properties.details:
Registry ID: 558
Species: subalpine fir (conifer)
Species rank: #3
Tree score: 243
Height 31.4 m · DBH 1.03 m · crown spread 14.2 m
Nearest town: Fernie
Location: Olivia Creek Trail
Ownership: Provincial land
Last measured: 7/13/2020
Site notes: The tree is a bit inconspicuous as a subalpine fir, as most of the surrounding trees are large Englemann spruce. The bark on this old tree was not easily distinguishable as a subalpine fir, but the branches swept right down close to the ground, allowing for tree species identification. Located on edge of an avalanche meadow, where a profusion of alpine flowers were in bloom, including: Sitka valerian, Forget-Me-Nots, stinging nettle, blue elderberry, clasping twisted stalk, yellow columbine, and silky phacelia. 
An adjacent 1.54 m. DBH Englemann Spruce was aged at 502 years old.
Access notes: The Olivia Creek Trail can be accessed by travelling up the Hartley Lake Rd. from Dicken Road. Hartley Lake Road is a narrow winding dirt road, but is passable under most conditions with a 2WD vehicle. Once you have passed the lake, below to the left, you are at the Hartley/Sulphur Creek Pass. Olivia Creek access is the second old road to the left, just before the road begins descending towards the Bull River. The old road can be quite overgrown, and will have large puddles to navigate around. This 4 km. road section can be driven in a 4WD if you are not worried about your paint job, and want to earn some more Kootenay Pinstripes. If you get lured into driving up this road, there are no good turn arounds until it can be too late. Using a bike, or hiking is recommended to get to the old sawdust pile, from where 1 km. further, on a less friendly road, connects you to the trailhead.

properties.title: Jeffy Dougy
properties.details:
Registry ID: 559
Species: interior Douglas-fir (conifer)
Species rank: #2
Tree score: 407
Height 49.5 m · DBH 1.87 m · crown spread 15.6 m
Nearest town: Fernie
Location: Elk R. / Morrissey Cr.
Ownership: Parks/reserves · Nature Conserv. of CA
Last measured: 7/26/2020
Site notes: Tree is the lone interior Douglas-fir observed in this small protected stand of western redcedar, hemlock, black cottonwood, and Englemann spruce. Definitely predates the surrounding trees. Located on the Elk River floodplain.
Access notes: Mt Broadwood Hertitage Conservancy.  If interested in visiting this site, drive on Highway #3,  16 km. west from Fernie, and turn left onto the Morrissey Road. The road crosses over the Elk River, then the CPR tracks, where you take the road to the right. Stay on the main road (River Road) where you will come to the Morrissey Creek bridge. Just before the bridge, a road to the right (the TransCanada Great Trail) leads down towards the Elk River. Stay to the left all the way down the road,  as there are many rights, until you reach a yellow gate at the CPR tracks. Park here and walk down the tracks a short distance to your right (north), where you will come into a large opening that is the hydro transmission powerline right of way. To your left, towards the Elk River, and through a cattle gate (close after passing through), you will begin to notice enormous cedar stumps, and dark forests lining either side of the right of way clearing. The Jeffy Dougy fir is located in the forest on the left. If you follow a small drainage channel upstream, keeping your eyes up, the top of this gnarly flowertop tree can be seen above the canopy.

Species: whitebark pine (conifer)
Species rank: #1
Tree score: 198
Height 24.4 m · DBH 0.85 m · crown spread 16 m
Nearest town: Sparwood
Location: Barnes Lake
Ownership: Tree Farm Lic. · Canfor
Last measured: 8/17/2020
Site notes: Many dead standing whitebark pines in this vicinity. Likely blister rust casualties. The remaining live trees appear to be somewhat healthy. Cores from tree were solid to the center. Trees estimated age is 350 years old. +/- 50 yrs.
Access notes: The site can be accessed by driving east on Highway #3 from the Highway #43 traffic lights in Sparwood for 11km. to the Coal Mountain /Michel Creek Road. This paved road continues for 22.6 km. to the Coal Mountain mine gate, where the Flathead FSR to the right leads to the next right turn-off at 4.4 km.. A new logging road and bridge have been built crossing Michel Creek, where you can either begin walking here, or continue on a very rough road for 800 m. to the trailhead. The unmarked old road on the west side of the landing is your route. After hiking for 2.5 km. you will come to an intersection. The left trail/road leads to Barnes Lake, while the right road climbs steeply up to Elliot Lake. If heading to Barnes Lake the trail continues for an additional 1.3 km. following along a beautiful alpine meadow, to where you will arrive at the south campsite.
The Whitebark Pine that was sampled, is located just beside the campsite.

properties.title: Moe's #1
properties.details:
Registry ID: 563
Species: western larch (conifer)
Species rank: #9
Tree score: 352
Height 54.5 m · DBH 1.34 m · crown spread 9 m
Nearest town: Kimberley
Location: Moe's Canyon Trail
Ownership: Provincial land · Kimberly Nordic Area
Last measured: 11/24/2019
Site notes: This tree is in a one ha patch of old growth of western larch/Douglas-fir/spruce growing in a flat area right at the south end of Moe's Canyon.  Logging occured in 2006 to the south and east of this patch and elsewhere within the Kimberley Nordic Trails area.  The patch contains at least 13 large trees over 100 cm DBH and eight of these trees are over 50m in height.  All the largest trees are western larch but there are two Douglas-fir trees scoring over 300 points.  This is the highest ranking tree found based on height, circumference and crown size.   The smaller mature western larch trees at the periphery of this area are well over 400 years old so this tree could be in the 600 - 800 yr range.
Access notes: Drive up Gerry Sorensen Way, past Kimberley Alpine Resort and continue until the road becomes North Star Drive. The Nordic Club is at the end of North StarDrive.  Take any of the fun trails around to the south end of the Centennial loop to Iker's landing.  Then take Landsem south.  About half way along Landsem look for a smaller trail marked Moe's Canyon/Magic Line.  Follow this steep up to the top.  You are now looking north at the old growth larch patch.  Magic line cuts right, to the east of the patch and Moe's Canyon Trail goes north through the patch past the Mussers Plateau Trail junction and continues north into Moe's Canyon.  Moe's #1 is just east of the trail, about 60m north of the Magic line junction.  This and the other tallest trees in Moes are also visible from the south end of Larch Loop Trail.

Site notes: This tree has a small burn scar at the base, a large burl at 18m, broken top at 39m and a Y-shaped live top.  This would be the highest ranking tree in this area if not for the broken top. It does have the largest circumference and crown size, and the most majestic look overall.

About half way along Landsem look for a smaller trail marked Moe's Canyon/Magic Line.  Follow this steep up to the top.  You are now looking north at the old growth larch patch.  Magic line cuts right, to the east of the patch and Moe's Canyon Trail goes north through the patch past the Mussers Plateau Trail junction and continues north into Moe's Canyon.  Moe's #1 is just east of the trail, about 60m north of the Magic line junction.  Moe's #3 is 35m further, 15m east of the trail. This and the other tallest trees in Moes are also visible from the south end of Larch Loop Trail.

Site notes: This tree is an absolute giant. It has a massive, burly base and a super thick trunk that towers skyward to a multi-forked top. The tree is up hill on the left above the road cut. Use GPS for final way-finding.

Species rank: #48
Tree score: 424
Height 44.5 m · DBH 2.16 m · crown spread 13.5 m
Nearest town: Revelstoke
Location: Goldstream FSR
Ownership: Tree Farm Lic. · 56 Revelstoke ComForCorp
Last measured: 9/13/2021
Site notes: Tree is a fairly solid and uniform diameter column with only a light flair and a full canopy. It is located in a beautiful valley bottom grove along the south side of the Goldstream River. The tree was one of the largest we found valley bottom up the Goldstream FSR. The grove is located at the confluence of a smaller stream entering into the river, contains wetland areas and shows evidence of annual flooding at high water.This grove is one of the bigger intact groves along the base of the valley. Most significant sized trees in this grove are in the 1.75 to 2 meter dbh range. The vegetation in the area is fairly lush with a good layer of Devils Club, however with sandy soil and areas that show evidence of frequent high water there are patches of more limited undergrowth. There is a fairly clear trail that runs from the Goldstream FSR to the tree and shows evidence of being used by both elk and people. A muddy, wetland area directly south of the tree shows evidence of being a well used elk bed.
Access notes: From Revelstoke drive 108 kn north on Hwy 23. Turn east on Goldstream FSR. Between km 31 and 32 on Goldsteam FSR stop before creek crossing. Tree is located approximately 200 meters from the road walking north.

properties.title: western redcedar · Registry 972
properties.details:
Registry ID: 972
Species: western redcedar (conifer)
Species rank: #55
Tree score: 390
Height 42.7 m · DBH 1.97 m · crown spread 8 m
Nearest town: Jaffray
Location: Dibble Creek
Ownership: Provincial land · Galloway Lumber
Last measured: 7/21/2021
Site notes: The measured tree is touching another large cedar at the base.  Both trees have forked stems at 3-5m.  The fork on the measured tree is dead.  This patch of trees contains several cedars in the 150-170cm range. This cedar old growth is, for now, fed by Dibble Glacier and is quite unique in the East Kootenay area.
Access notes: Driving Directions:From Bull River, travel north on the Wardner Fort Steele Road. Turn east on Bull River Road. In 8.5km the road intersects with Bull River FSR. Turn left (northeast) on Bull River FSR. The trailhead is approximately 10km from this junction, on the left, at a pullout just past the Dibble Cr bridge.  The trail follows a deactivated road for about 3km.  Then steeper single track for 1km to a tributary and the old growth cedar stands starting at about 1260m elev. along the east side of the creek.  The measured cedar is at about 5km, above the trail, just before the first slide path.

properties.title: western larch · Registry 973
properties.details:
Registry ID: 973
Species: western larch (conifer)
Species rank: #13
Tree score: 326
Height 46.3 m · DBH 1.36 m · crown spread 7 m
Nearest town: Kimberley
Location: Horse Barn Valley
Ownership: Provincial land · Canfor
Last measured: 10/14/2021
Site notes: The tree is located in the Horse Barn Valley Interpretive Forest which is managed by the Kimberley Nature Park Society. This tree has scorched bark and a scar running 8m up the top side of the tree.  It has a large fork at 16m and a broken top/fork at 40m. It is growing on a steep sidehill and is leaning almost over the trail. This tree is just North of a nice patch of old growth cedar.
Access notes: Horse Barn Valley Interpretive Forest. Driving Directions:   High-ground-clearance vehicle is recommended. From the Kimberley Riverside Campground and RV Resort it is 8.9 kilometres to the parking area. From the campground, drive west on the paved St. Mary Lake Road for 4.1 km. Turn right on the Matthew Creek Forestry Road and just before the 2km sign turn right again on a narrower, rougher gravel road marked with a HBV signpost. After about 1.5km veer left then right to keep climbing to the parking area and kiosks.   The Western Larch tree is a short walk from the kiosk in on Talus Trail. Cross a small bridge, then a board walk and 50m along the larch is on your left, at a small Queen's Cup interpretive sign.

properties.title: Target
properties.details:
Registry ID: 974
Species: western white pine (conifer)
Species rank: #1
Tree score: 407
Height 56 m · DBH 1.73 m · crown spread 12 m
Nearest town: Cherryville
Location: Greenbush Lake
Ownership: Tree Farm Lic. · Tolko
Last measured: 6/25/2021
Site notes: This tree stands out amongst the surrounding forest. Both the height, and shadowy girth are very impressive. The tree had a blue "O" spray painted on the trunk. This mark indicated that I was not the first person to visit this tree. The follow up search revealed that a forester with Tolko had marked this tree 12 years earlier.  LiDar imagery provided by Tolko (available if requested) showed this tree poking out of the data.
Access notes: The Sugar Lake FSR heads out of Cherryville extending along the lake, past Monashee Provincial Park to the east, passes the Upper Shuswap River Ecological Reserve (42 km marker), then comes to a junction of the Blanket FSR to the right. Turn onto Blanket FSR. The road climbs up above Greenbush Lake, and the tree is just below the road after the  first switchback.

properties.title: The Mammoth
properties.details:
Registry ID: 975
Species: western redcedar (conifer)
Species rank: #14
Tree score: 539
Height 42.9 m · DBH 3.14 m · crown spread 12 m
Nearest town: Fernie
Location: Cedar Valley
Ownership: Private land · Island Lake Lodge
Last measured: 8/23/2021
Site notes: Included in the trees height is a 4.0 m. dead spire top. The tree is surrounded with heavy underbrush, making accessibility somewhat difficult. The bulbous base of the tree is typical of the many old cedars growing in this area.
Access notes: Accessed from the Mount Fernie Park road off of Highway 3 near Fernie, you drive through the campground, and follow the gravel Island Lake access road until you arrive at their first parking area and gate. If the Lodge is open for summer guests the gate will be open. Otherwise you can walk / ski or ride your bike up the road or provided trails.
About 4 km up the road a second trailhead parking area for the Old Growth trail is on the right. You can park here, and walk up the road about another 50 m and an old spur to the right (the winter road) leads up another 50 m where the "Mammoth" is hiding in the bushes on the left.

properties.title: Grandmother of the Eagle
properties.display: Grandmother of the Eagle · western redcedar
properties.details:
Registry ID: 976
Species: western redcedar (conifer)
Species rank: #18
Tree score: 525
Height 34.5 m · DBH 3.21 m · crown spread 18 m
Nearest town: Malakwa
Location: Eagle River
Ownership: Parks/reserves · Eagle River Nature Park
Last measured: 9/17/2021
Site notes: Tree is luxuriating in the riparian area of the Eagle River, and enjoys lots of space allowing for the impressive spread of the branches. The flat, floodplain, and watersoaked surroundings provide ideal growing conditions for these big cedar trees.
Access notes: The Eagle River Nature Park is located on the opposite side of Highway 1 from  the Yard Creek Provincial Park campground in Malakwa (12 km east of Sicamous). This is a section of divided highway, so turning onto the Malakwa north frontage road is a bit challenging. Once on the north frontage road head to the west end where the trailhead parking lot is located. The 6 km loop trail has a few cedar groves, with the Grandmother of the Eagle tree being at the furthest out on the loop trail.

properties.title: western larch · Registry 1015
properties.details:
Registry ID: 1015
Species: western larch (conifer)
Species rank: #6
Tree score: 354
Height 56 m · DBH 1.32 m · crown spread 8 m
Nearest town: Jaffray
Location: Bloom Creek
Ownership: Provincial land · Canfor
Last measured: 11/19/2021
Site notes: This tree has some scorch at the bottom, but is otherwise quite intact.  Remnants of a whorl of large branches is evident at about 6m up.  Two other larch trees are within 5-6m of this one, forming quite a trio!  The two largest of the three are within 5m of a tributary to Bloom Creek.  The other large larch (128cm DBH) is leaning downstream and would be close to 55m if growing straight up. The smaller (~1m) larch has a broken top, totald height is about 35m.  Another large larch lies toppled over the creek, making a natural bridge just upstream.
A proposed bridge location and road centre line is marked out about 20m upstream and upslope from the two closer trees of the trio.  
The surrounding riparian area contains a range of species - spruce, balsam, cedar, hemlock and Douglas fir but all the largest trees are western larch up and down the creek for about 100m, with large live trees, short and tall snags, and down trees. Most of these larch are in the 80cm diam range.
Access notes: From Jaffray or Elko drive down to Kikomun Creek Prov. Park.  Take Teepee Cr Rd. west across Koocanusa Lake, past the campground/boat access. Then head south on Caven Cr FSR (starting at 15.5 km).  At 32.5 km turn left onto Bloom FSR, at 42.5 turn right onto Middle Bloom and park just past the 45 km sign.  It is a short hike down to the creek through ~50 yr old Lodgepole pine second growth.

Access notes: Gilnockie Provincial Park and Ecological Reserve are a long ways from anywhere. Site notes: Western hemlocks of this enormity are not that common, generally succumbing to old age, rot, blowdown, or casual chainsaw death. The sheltered high elevation environment seems well suited for this big tree. This is the biggest tree found in this grove, but there are likely some larger ones to be found if getting off trail is your thing.
Access notes: From Highway 3 when travelling west from Creston, and right before the yellow avalanche closure gate is a large pull-out parking area on your left, where some unobtrusive trail signs are attached to the trees. Situated quite high up on the trees so as to not disappear as the snow pack gets deeper. A trail heads down to where it crosses Summit Creek, and then a loop configuration allows you to chose your direction on the 1.3 km route. I like to walk it both ways, as new delights are revealed every time.

Site notes: This spruce is truly out of this world! It must have grown over top of something a long time ago, creating this massive, burly, rootball base that if you measure it there, would be 4.7m wide. We measured it around the narrower trunk above. There is a noteable 'knuckle' window that sticks out off the side and reconnects with the tree creating a window. So strange!! Really one of the coolest trees either of us had ever seen before.
Access notes: Starting from Holberg, take San Joseph Main towards the coast. Turn left onto Raft Main. Take your first right onto a small side road (semi-over grown with alders). A short ways down you will see the current #1 Sitka spruce tree on your right. Park here and admire that tree before heading into the forest on the opposite side of the road (choose your own adventure as to how to get in there). Use GPS coordinates to track down the tree. An alternate route would be to bushwhack in off of Palmerston Main.

Site notes: A beautiful Sitka spruce tree growing in a Wildlife Habitat Area along the Keith River near Side Bay. Legend has it loggers refused to cut down this patch of forest given it's impressive nature while the entire surrounding areas were clearcut in the 1980's. Today an island of old-growth exists here. Site notes: This cedar is absolutely enormous. It's huge, riveted trunk looks like the chest of a humpback whale. A number of large limbs then burst skyward, creating healthy and bushy crown. Unfortunately, however, like Big Lonely Doug, it stands alone in a clearcut from 2019. It's likely that its health will suffer now that the forest is gone around it. After surviving for many, many centuries, only time will tell if it will make it to the end of the next one.

*There is a notable spiral cedar within viewing distance of this one and another impressive lone cedar a bit further up the road as well.

Registry ID: 1111

Site notes: From Prince George Drive East on Hwy 16 to Dome Creek Rd. East of The Ancient Forest/Chun T'oh Whudujut Provincial Park and Protected Area. *12.5 km After the Dome Creek Rd. Hwy Intersection (Joe Boo's Mobile Eatery) there is a small turnaround and garbage disposal location on the North Side of Hwy. This is a Good Parking Spot. If you pass Walker Creek FSR you have gone too far.* Tree is located on the South (SSW) side of Hwy, roughly 80-100 m from the parking area and 40-60 m from the brushed road edge. Hikers must climb up the steep ditch embankment and into the forest, minor elevation gain after entry into Mature Stand Area. System of very large Trees and Alli's Hollow are along a small plateau between the Hwy and a Rocky Ridge above, leading to a Silviculture regen area.
Access notes: Minor amount of blowdown, regen close to Hwy but forest floor and canopy open up before rocky outcrop uphill. Unknown cultural history.  Area has potential Culturally Modified Trees, and has been previously surveyed for Timber and most likely Ecotyping.  Very old flagging found throughout, near potential CMTs and large timber stands.  Multiple human-made "test" holes found throughout the forest, as well as a potentially "stripped" Cedar tree.  Area was part of a 2008 push by local organizations to introduce an investigation by the Forestry Board (Dome Creek area) as to the impact of logging in ICH stands in the Robson Valley "Funnel" and as a result an extensive Old Growth Management Area Plan was introduced.  This "island" is an "Ancient" area (as B.C.Forestmap.com age class) which was left out of OGMA areas, deemed fragmented due to previous logging operations. Area is known for Caribou.  SARA listed species found within and above (previously documented on inaturalist) the "island" such as Nephroma occultum (Cryptic paw) and potential for Smokers Lung (Lobaria retigera) due to noted sites nearby.  Beautiful highway site, tree is visible from the road.  In summertime the area will be abundant with Devils Club.  Easy to get to and a magnificent little nook and a pleasant day hike area.

properties.title: Oyster River Giant
properties.details:
Registry ID: 1144
Species: black cottonwood (broadleaf)
Species rank: #22
Tree score: 376
Height 49.7 m · DBH 1.61 m · crown spread 16.9 m
Nearest town: Oyster River
Location: Fisherman' Trail
Ownership: Parks/reserves · Oyster R. Nature Park
Last measured: 6/5/2022
Site notes: The tree has an extremely columnar trunk with no noticeable taper until the first branching at approxumately 25-30m. The tree appears to be in good health with a nearly symmetrical radial crown. There is what appears to be a small 15-20cm diameter secondary trunk originating near the base of the tree that has self-grafted to the vastly larger main trunk. It has been completely incorporated intomthe main stem and cannot be differentiated beyind the 8-10m height on the mainstem. I would consider it to be an integral part of the tree. The tree appears to be in very good health with no broken limbs or apparent cavities in the main stem.
Access notes: From Highway 19A turn onto Glenmore Road. Continue on Glenmore until you reach the Oyster River Nature Park parking lot. The tree is located only a few metres from the trail as you enter the Oyster River Nature Park from the bottom parking lot near the old Fishermens Lodge Pub. It is on the left hand side of the trail and is very noticable.

properties.title: Twister
properties.details:
Registry ID: 1145
Species: western redcedar (conifer)
Height 30.2 m · DBH 2.4 m
Nearest town: Crescent Spur
Location: Goat R. Canyon Trail
Ownership: Parks/reserves · West Twin PP
Last measured: 6/4/2022
Site notes: Found in a wet ancient forest in the ICH BEC zone, this tree was the second largest in the grove. Surrounded by devils club and ferns.
Access notes: From Crescent Spur, drive south on Loos Road towards Highway 16. Turn left on Highway 16 and drive southeast for 8.9 km towards the Goat River bridge. Just before the highway bridge over the Goat River, park on the left (north) side of the highway at the Goat River Rest Area. From the rest area, follow instructions for "Goat River Canyon Trail" on Trailpeak.                  the Goat River Rest Area. From the rest area, follow instructions for "Goat River Canyon Trail" on Trailpeak. 

The trail is accessed by an old road on the south side of Highway 16, 1/2km before the Goat River bridge and rest area. The old road is easily missed by those driving on Highway 16, because of the steep drop it takes off the highway. If you do not have a 4-WD vehicle, it is best to park at the Goat River rest area and walk west on the south side of Highway 16 to spot the rough access road. If you drive down the old road, there is a small clearing a short ways down with room to park.The hike initially follows the old road. You will cross a rough wooden bridge over a creek. Shortly afterwards, you will reach a fork in the road where the right side is very overgrown. Take the left fork. A short distance after this, there is a second fork in the road, where an ATV trail continues to the right and the left side appears less worn-in. At this second fork, follow the left (less worn-in) side. After a minute or so, take the trail on the left leading away from the old road and into the forest (it should be flagged). From here, the trail is easy to follow. You will stay on the plateau before crossing a stream and descending towards the canyon. After the stream is where the very old trees are located.GPS Coordinates:- Old road off Highway 16: 53.4924063, -120.6176087- Goat River Canyon (trail end point, for reference, to ensure one is hiking in the correct direction): 53.4772961, -120.6406700.

Hike down the trail almost to the end. To get to the tree requires about 30m of bushwacking from the trail.

Nearest town: Golden
Location: Smith Creek
Ownership: Provincial land
Last measured: 9/19/2022
Site notes: The tree is somewhat solitary, and appears to have been graciously left behind. With huge limbs spreading out above as cedars. We circumnavigated around its girth, where the Interior sized D-Tape couldnt wrap the entire circumference. Our explorations down below towards the creek turned up some considerable sized western red cedars, western hemlocks, and a notable Engelmann spruce. This region is worthy of further explorations, where myths of even larger cedars are whispered by the locals.
Access notes: From Golden BC drive west 45 km on TransCanada Highway 1, as you start to climb up from the Columbia River bridge crossing, keep an eye to the right for a sign that says Kinbasket Lake Resort, turn off of the highway here. The rough gravel road (Columbia West FSR) descends steeply down to where the now closed Resort is situated at the Beaver River bridge crossing. Set your odometer to 0 here. Drive 58.7 km to where the Smith Creek drainage crosses the road. At this switchback, the very overgrown spur follows the drainage to where the road is obstructed by a small landslide. We had to back down from here, so best to just park at the junction and walk up to the tree. It is only about 850 m until this massive tree shows up on the left side of the road. You cant miss it!

properties.title: McIver 8
properties.details:
Registry ID: 1185
Species: coastal Douglas-fir (conifer)
Species rank: #81
Tree score: 499
Height 66 m · DBH 2.18 m · crown spread 14.2 m
Nearest town: Woss
Location: Sebalhal R./McIver Cr.
Ownership: Provincial land
Last measured: 10/6/2022
Site notes: McIver #8 is in good health. It is largest diameter tree amongst a number of scattered Douglas fir vets in the 60m to 71m tall range within a natural fire induced second growth. The fire was recorded as 1930, and is verbally recognized to be originating from a seasonal fish smoking site, belonging to "the river people" within the greater traditional territory of the Namgis First Nation, at the mouth of McIver Creek & Sebalhal Creek on Vernon Lake.
Access notes: Drive from Woss 10km south on highway 19 to the Mt.Cain turnoff going onto the Nimpkish Main south, following to the Sebalhal Main. Drive the Sebalhal Main to the McIver Main.
Drive the McIver main to across the McIver river bridge and then turn right onto first spur right off the McIver Main. Drive 600m to end of spur and walk into the timber to tree.

properties.title: Sutton Sentinel
properties.details:
Registry ID: 1187
Species: amabilis fir (conifer)
Species rank: #1
Tree score: 431
Height 67.7 m · DBH 1.64 m · crown spread 8 m
Nearest town: Woss
Location: Sutton Road UWR
Ownership: Tree Farm Lic. · 37 UWR
Last measured: 10/24/2022
Site notes: Tree is showing sings of crown die back due to extreme age. It is growing on flat ground on high bench flood plain above the Nimpkish River near the junction of Sutton Creek and the Kla-anch wetlands. The area has high Elk useage.  The stand is very unique upper valley, CWHmm1 Amabilis dominant stand with multiple Amabalis well over 65m in height and we believed at least 2 may be taller than this nomination, but it is difficult to get the height of the others due to the heavy understory and brush.

The tallest tree previously measured adjacent to these, but now logged, was 248 ft tall. Because of this previously biggest trees loss, Chris Bowden-Green approached John Deal of Canfor to protect the remaining large Balsam within a proposed Elk Winter Range, due to its uniqueness as one of the last remaining old growth valley bottom Amabalis stands.
Access notes: From Woss head south 12km on Highway 19 to the Mt.Cain turnoff and proceed onto the Nimpkish Main south. Travel south 27km on the Nimpkish Main past the Vernon Camp turnoff continuing on the Nimpkish Main until you reach the next left which is the Sutton Road turnoff. Go aproximately 1km on the Sutton Main until you will see the top of the tree above the advanced regen on the south low side of the road.

properties.title: western redcedar · Registry 1200
properties.details:
Registry ID: 1200
Species: western redcedar (conifer)
Height 37.9 m · DBH 3.15 m
Nearest town: Dome Creek
Location: Driscoll Ridge
Ownership: Provincial land · MOT Quarry Reserve
Last measured: 6/17/2022
Site notes: The stand is located on level mid-slope bench on the north face of Driscoll Ridge. Trees are growing on a wet site with ground vegetation dominated by Devil's Club, located in the ICHvk2 biogeoclimatic zone. The tree is healthy with abundant "wolf-tree" (downward sweeping) branches in the lower canopy. The broken top is consistent with nearly all the old trees on this site.
Access notes: Drive east 110 km (ca. 1 hour) from Prince George to the Ancient Forest/Chun T'oh Whudujut Provincial Park trail parking lot (marking with highway pullout signs). From the Ancient Forest trail pullout drive west 5 km to the entry site for the Ministry of Transport quarry, found on the south side of the road (look for locked gate on access road).  Park on the roadside or on the edge of the quarry pull-off and hike up the old Driscoll Ridge trail. The trail is heavily overgrown with Devil's Club and alder, watch for the red trail markers on trees (the old trail route also shows on most GPS map apps).  If the lower quarry site is active access on the old Driscoll Ridge trail is not allowed.

The trail is heavily overgrown with Devil's Club and alder, watch for the red trail markers on trees (the old trail route also shows on most GPS map apps).  If the lower quarry site is active access on the old Driscoll Ridge trail is not allowed.
properties.site_notes: The stand is located on level mid-slope bench on the north face of Driscoll Ridge. Trees are growing on a wet site with ground vegetation dominated by Devil's Club, located in the ICHvk2 biogeoclimatic zone.  The tree has a noticeable line of burls ca 2 m off the ground extending across the north side of the tree.

Registry ID: 1222
Species: western redcedar (conifer)
Species rank: #10
Tree score: 568
Height 51.3 m · DBH 3.15 m · crown spread 12.4 m
Nearest town: Revelstoke
Location: Frisby Creek Valley
Ownership: Provincial land
Last measured: 10/10/2022
Site notes: Tree has significant graduated multidirectional lean. Tree is on edge of landslide area and has some mechanical damage and is surrounded by avalanche debris. This area is prone to avalanche due to steep slopes above.

The tree is located in a spectacular contiguous old growth area in the Frisby Creek drainage that has not been significantly impacted by logging. There has been some shake bolting and selective logging lower in the valley. The valley is towered over by steep slopes and the tree is on a bench situated above a lower bench along Frisby Creek and below steep slopes leading into the alpine. Moist and lush area. Lots of Devil's club and moss, abundant mushrooms. Lots of moose activity and bear dens in the area.
Access notes: Boat access only traveling west across Revelstoke Lake. Good launch point at Carnes Creek Recreation Site accessed via Hwy 23 north of Revelstoke. Tree is located approximately 2 to 2.5 km up a flagging marked trail . Trail is accessed from a small flagged drainage approx 500 m north of the mouth of Frisby Creek. Accessing area through Frisby Creek not recommended.

properties.title: Wye Fir
properties.details:
Registry ID: 1225
Species: coastal Douglas-fir (conifer)
Species rank: #13
Tree score: 636
Height 82.8 m · DBH 2.78 m · crown spread 24.8 m
Nearest town: Youbou
Location: Pipe Dream
Ownership: Tree Farm Lic. · 44 OGMA
Last measured: 11/19/2022
Site notes: A very healthy tree, showing vigourous apical growth and a dense crown that can be seen from the road. It has a high, narrow fork with two co-dominant leaders, giving it a truly remarkable crown spread. The tree is situated on a moderate slope near the edge of a seasonal creek ravine. In a stand of exceptional trees, it still stands out from 50 meters away in all directions as remarkable.
Access notes: Notes current to Dec. 2022. No gates or deactivated roads. Directions from Cassy's Coffee House in Youbou. Travel 24.6km west along North Shore Road and turn right onto Nitinat Main. After 4.1km, turn left onto NT2. Cross the bridge at 1.1km and stay left at the fork at 1.3km. Stay left at the fork at 2.3km. Stay right at the fork at 7.4km. Stay left at the fork at 9.1km. At 9.7km, turn right onto the branch road. At 500m stay left at the fork. At 1.2km, stay left at the fork. At 1.9km, turn left onto the spur. Follow road until recent cutblock on both sides of the road (logged 2019). Park at a pullout and hike uphill through the cutblock to access Pipe Dream! The Wye fir is near the northern end of Pipe Dream. The most direct route is to continue driving along the road until the end of the next regenerating cutblock (logged 2006). You can park around 48.935442, -124.587609. Hike up through the regen along the seasonal creek 60m until you reach the old growth. Follow the lip of the ravine uphill for another 90m until you reach the Wye fir.

Like several trees in the stand, it has two distinct types of bark occuring on the upslope and downslope sides of the tree. The tree is situated on a gentle slope, with a cluster of three large firs just 30m north and uphill.

Site notes: The Memory Tree is possibly the tallest tree remaining in the Cowichan Valley, based on the publicly-available LiDAR data. It is situated at the base of a moderate slope above a bench with several good sized redcedars, in a dark and spacious stand. There are two other large (>2m DBH) firs just above the Memory Tree as well. This tree supports a large forked crown, giving it a very ovoid stem that, from the broad side, looks even larger than its 2.35m DBH would suggest.
Access notes: From the Glenora Trails parking lot, take the connector onto the Trans Canada Trail and turn right, towards the Holt Creek Trestle. After about 2.5km on this trail, you can see the Memory Tree and two other large, old firs sticking out above the second growth canopy by looking west through a cutblock (logged 2013) on the south side of the trail. After another 300m (2.8km total), enter into the second growth stand to the south of the trail and bushwhack 160m to the Memory Tree. Try to stay close to the edge of the forest, as there are a couple wet areas with devil's club further in.

Site notes: This spruce is absolutely phenominal and perhaps now the largest known overall in the Carmanah Valley. I boasts a thick, towering trunk that puts it in a league and likely age class of its own compared to other large spruce trees in the area. It also has one of the most dynamic and sprawling canopies. The main trunk breaks into two main stems which then also have multiple iterations of their own. From a top down perspective, the canopy of this one tree appears to be of 3-4 individual trees. This is one of the most rewarding and noteworthy big tree finds in a long time.

Height 74.6 m · DBH 1.85 m · crown spread 12 m
Nearest town: Sayward
Location: White River FSR
Ownership: Parks/reserves · White River PP
Last measured: 10/5/2022
Site notes: Touted as the "Cathedral Grove of the North.  The tree is within the protected area of the White River Provincial Park, which is a narrow linear strip of preserved old-growth, with extensive harvesting visual all around it. The Douglas-fir, tree #1292, is right beside this short trail, before you get to the river. The western redcedar, tree #1293, is upstream, off trail, through some flat, but deadfall barriered ground.  The Sitka spruce, tree #1294, is very close to the western redcedar.
Access notes: Turning west off of Highway 19, directly across from the Sayward exit, you will find yourself on the Salmon River Main. Accessing the park is not that straight forward, as there is no signage, and the White River FSR is somewhat off direction from the paved Salmon River Main, which lured me off course for about 6 km before realizing that the river was on the wrong road I was supposed to be on. Backtracking, I found where I missed the turn-off at the junction. The rough gravel road rises steeply from the Salmon River valley, where at the 17 km marker a junction where the road goes down to a bridge crossing the White River, is not the right direction, stay left on the Victoria Main for a further 6 km, where the Park Boundary sign is your first indication that you are getting close to your destination. A short distance further, and an obscure (facing in the wrong direction of travel) sign directs you towards a short trail that leads you through the big Douglas-fir trees towards the river.

A short distance further, and an obscure (facing in the wrong direction of travel) sign directs you towards a short trail that leads you through the big Douglas-fir trees towards the river.

Access notes: The 8.4 km access trail climbs 653 m vertical gain to a maximum elevation of 2830 m. You will be glad to get your legs stretched out after the long 29 km drive up the Glacier Creek FSR. Following the Duncan FSR from Argenta to the well signed right turn onto Glacier FSR is where the bone rattling begins, but once you become surrounded by the massive glaciated peaks, all discomfort disappears. Once at the parking lot, the trail switchbacks up steeply through ESSF forest, where at about 6 km you emerge into the larch studded, namesake meadows.  The tree can be seen above, to the left after you cross a bridge over a small creek. Following up through the gully you will see two large, ancient sentinels on the rocky ground above, the tree to the right #1327, and the larger more scraggy tree is # 977 "Grand Daddy Subby". There appear to be quite a few of these very old sub-alpine larches dotting the exposed ground in the meadow, so further big tree exploration of this beautiful sub-alpine area is warranted.

Registry ID: 1343
Species: coastal Douglas-fir (conifer)
DBH 2.37 m
Nearest town: Port Renfrew
Location: Loup Creek
Ownership: Forest Lic. · Qala:yit Com. For. OGMA
Last measured: 4/29/2023
Site notes: Loup Trident is ancient and decrepit, and seems extremely unstable. The crown is generally healthy, with incredible spiral grain and two large forks flanking a dead top that give it a trident appearance. Most of the centre of the tree is rotted out with very soft and hollow wood, and one side has only a strip of living bark tissue supporting it, which is completely separated from the wood. It is on a low slope near a couple other large firs just above the creek.
Access notes: From Port Renfrew, travel north towards Lake Cowichan. After crossing the Deering bridge, turn left to start down Gordon Main and proceed for 23km. Turn left onto Truck Road 10 and proceed for 5.2km. Turn left and cross the bridge over Loup Creek. Immediately turn left and follow the road until it ends after approximately 150m. Walk down the old FSR for about 2km, then bushwhack to the tree. Be aware that there are several seasonal and perennial streams that you will need to wade across while following the old FSR.

properties.title: The Darkside Cedar
properties.details:
Registry ID: 1361

Nearest town: Youbou

Site notes: The Darkside Cedar is a dark and robust. It is potentially comprised of two separate trees growing close together. It stands with a lean near the South West corner of Chewhat Lake. The Darkside Cedar is a dark and robust and suspected to be two separate trees growing close together. It stands with a lean near the South West corner of Cheewhat Lake.  It is located in a rather densely vegetated area, on a low angled slope, in the SW area of Cheewhat Lake.  The Cheewhat Lake area is a well known hotspot for western red cedar including some of Canada's largest known specimens.  Located near the Eastern boundary of the Pacific Rim NP and 10 km from the Pacific Coast, this wilderness area sees abundant precipitation and little natural disturbance, allowing for grand and ancient forest stands to persist. The region has been inhabited by various members of the Nuu-Chah-nulth Clan for centuries and contains many CMT's (culturally modified trees) and other archaeological sites.
Access notes: Access is from the North end of Cheewhat Lake. Please be aware that this is a trail-less wilderness area. Access to this and other areas on the West side of the Lake require strong prepared parties who are experienced at navigating  very challenging forested terrain. Only recommended to those who are familiar with this particular region. Please be advised that this is an ACTIVE logging area, follow suitably safe driving techniques and be vigilant and courteous to other road users. It is advised to only visit this area on weekends when logging activities are minimal. This is a remote area without cellular reception so plan your trip accordingly. Input your coordinates before you leave home. In general the gravel road driving is reasonable for most vehicles, top up your fuel and bring a full sized spare tire along for this trip.

Site notes: This tree is in excellent condition, other than having lost much of its upper crown quite some time ago. I remain convinced that this region warrants thorough exploration, as we were able to view other trees of similar size in this grove. Not far from this specimen are the remnants of the largest cedar we found, easily over 2.00 metres in diameter, I estimated. Its not unusual for yellow cedars such as these to be at least 1000 years old, and some are much older. Wildlife values for this area are exceptionally high, and the forest is regularly frequented by elk and black bear.
Access notes: 4x4 with good clearance required!  From Halfmoon Bay head east towards Trout Lake Road. Head north up Trout Lake Road. Around 5.5km, turn east (right) on Carlson Mainline towards Carlson Lake. At around 1.5km turn east (right) and head up an old, washed out road between 2 cut blocks. Follow this road for about 1.3km until you reach a fork. Take the road on the left that heads north up towards Spipiyus Provincial Park. Stay on this road for about 4.5km before reaching a 4 way. Turn right (east) and consider parking before the next cross ditch between the 2 small lakes. Enter the forest on the other side of this cross ditch. The tree is up on a little raised area with a small slope down to another small lake on the east side of it.

properties.title: The Big Tree
properties.details:
Registry ID: 1376
Species: coastal Douglas-fir (conifer)
Species rank: #40
Tree score: 571
Height 57.3 m · DBH 2.97 m · crown spread 19.7 m
Nearest town: Port Alberni
Location: McBride Cr./Gr. Cen. L.
Ownership: Parks/reserves · Strathcona PP
Last measured: 9/29/2023
Site notes: The tree is located in a large intact stand of old growth on a tributary of McBride Creek. It is growing on a broad bench that sits about 2 meters above the tributary. this bench sits at the base of a low mountain (650 meters) on the north side. Local knowledge tells of snow remaining in the area until early July most years. The stand is comprised of predominantly Pacific Silver Fir (Abies amabalis) with large Douglas-fir veterans scattered throughout. The tree displays little taper up to the height where the upper portion has been broken off. The tree displays good health and appears to be growing vigourously with no outward signs of rot or decay.
Core sampling of this tree produced an age of 1551 years, which could be one of the oldest known living Douglas-fir. The tree was discovered by long-time Port Alberni logging brothers Alvin and Gunny Brown. As family stories tell, the two bothers could not bring themselves to fall this giant as it was so much larger than any trees they had ever come across. Both are now deceased and their great-nephew, Rob Cole, wished to nominate this tree in their names.

The directions to 1177 are: From Golden BC drive west 45 km on TransCanada Highway 1, as you start to climb up from the Columbia River bridge crossing, keep an eye to the right for a sign that says Kinbasket Lake Resort, turn off of the highway here. The rough gravel road (Columbia West FSR) descends steeply down to where the now closed Resort is situated at the Beaver River bridge crossing. Set your odometer to 0 here. Height 43.6 m · DBH 1.04 m · crown spread 11.1 m
