Location: Kimberley Nature Park
Ownership: Provincial land · City of Kimberley
Last measured: 10/26/2023
Site notes: Tree has a large fire scar and a 4m dead top. Fairly large gnarly branches and burls give it an ancient look. Needles have piled up at the base of the tree since the last fire, forming a thick layer. An 80cm/36m Douglas-fir is just 5m up the slope.  The tree in is a Williamson's Sapsucker (WISA) Wildlife Habitat Area within Kimberley Nature Park. Critical WISA habitat includes large wildlife trees like this western larch as suitable nest trees, large snags and downed wood for ant foraging and mid-sized Douglas-fir for sap wells. The WHA is being treated for fuels - small trees and ladder fuel removal will hopefully protect the WISA habitat over time.  The tree was discovered by the Wildsight Youth Climate Corps crew.
Access notes: From the Kimberley Riverside Campground take the Campground Trail up to Jimmy Russel Road. Follow it up and turn right on Duck Pond Trail. Follow Duck Pond up to junction with Skid Road Trail. The western larch is about 200m N-NW from this point, about 50m up from the base of the hill.

properties.details:
Registry ID: 1419
Species: coastal Douglas-fir (conifer)
Species rank: #17
Tree score: 625
Height 86.9 m · DBH 2.63 m · crown spread 17.5 m
Nearest town: Youbou
Location: Pipe Dream
Ownership: Tree Farm Lic.
Last measured: 8/25/2023
Site notes: This extremely tall fir is located at the edge of a very small bench within a steep ravine near the edge of an old clearcut. Although the protection of the ravine hasgiven rise to a fair number of tall firs, this one stands well above the rest in both height and diameter. The top of the tree appears to have blown off some time ago, suggesting this tree was once possibly taller than 90m.
Access notes: Notes current to Dec. 2022. No gates or deactivated roads. Directions from Cassy's Coffee House in Youbou. Travel 24.6km west along North Shore Road and turn right onto Nitinat Main. After 4.1km, turn left onto NT2. Cross the bridge at 1.1km and stay left at the fork at 1.3km. Stay left at the fork at 2.3km. Stay right at the fork at 7.4km. Stay left at the fork at 9.1km. At 9.7km, turn right onto the branch road. At 500m stay left at the fork. At 1.2km, stay left at the fork. At 1.9km, turn left onto the spur. Follow road until recent cutblock on both sides of the road (logged 2019). This tree is on the far side of a fairly large ravine from the rest of the stand. Suggest hiking in through the third growth/riparian corridor. Some sections are very steep and loose, so use extreme caution.

properties.title: South Creek Giant
properties.details:
Registry ID: 1443
Species: western redcedar (conifer)
Species rank: #15
Tree score: 745
Height 49.2 m · DBH 4.63 m · crown spread 12.8 m
Nearest town: Pemberton
Location: South Creek
Ownership: Provincial land
Last measured: 10/27/2019
Site notes: The tree appears to be healthy and has long green branches and foliage which drape to the ground. There is one large burl located 182 centimetres above the ground on the southeast side of the trunk. The stem is forked once mid-height on the stem, and a second fork is present near the very top of the tree. Of these three stems, the tallest is still alive and the other two appear dead. Vertical surface-level scratches and scars in the bark on the lower trunk indicate potential wildlife use. The surrounding subalpine ecosystem is a shaded valley bottom with a southeast slope angle of 5-10 degrees and a small flattening where the tree itself stands. South Creek lies southeast of the tree, 200 metres away, and the tree itself stands at the bottom of a large avalanche path, indicated by the presence of dense slide alder and the absence of large trees. A small, seasonal creek runs near the tree. The surrounding forest has minimal understory, except for the presence of devil's club and slide alder. This forest has many other large trees of note.
Access notes: From Pemberton, drive up Pemberton Meadows Road until a large gate on the Lillooet South FSR at km 2. From this gate, hike or bike up the Lillooet South FSR until you cross South Creek, and turn left onto South Creek Road which branches south off the main line immediately after the bridge. Follow South Creek Road into the South Creek valley until you come to a landslide, which has completely destroyed the road and bridge. Leave the road and hike down to the creek, and walk upriver until you come across a log crossing and the partially destroyed bridge. Use these with extreme caution and only at low water. Cross the creek to continue on South Creek Road, which now runs along the south side of the valley. Follow this road, which gets progressively more bushy, until you reach a second crossing back to the north side of the valley. This bridge is also out, but a log crossing can be found 360 metres downstream. Once you are again on the north side of South Creek, follow the road to its end. Alternatively, open areas on the last 1 kilometre of road may offer a potential helicopter landing area. Hike through clearcut and then open forest for 220 metres (170 metres from the edge of the clearcut), heading southwest, until you reach the bottom of a large avalanche path. The tree is located at the bottom of this avalanche path and its size makes it unmistakable from other large trees nearby.

Site notes: This fire scarred veteran remains in exceptionally good health, with a very robust, distinctive crown. It may be the largest firs in the Nanaimo area.
Access notes: From Cedar, begin at the parking area at the end of Nicola Road. Hike the Cable Bay Trail to Cable Bay, then continue on toward Joan Point and Dodds Narrows. About 5 to ten minutes later look for a spur that turns right off the main trail (marked by a stump, see photo).  Follow this path uphill for another 5 to 10 minutes, using the waypoint provided to guide you to the tree, which will appear on the left side of the trail. The tree is situated on private land, 40 metres uphill on the spur trail.  The landowner currently allows public access.  Watch out for people riding horses as the trail is also used by equestrians.

properties.title: Grandalf the Fir
properties.details:
Registry ID: 1453
Species: grand fir (conifer)
Species rank: #1
Tree score: 333
Height 43.5 m · DBH 1.45 m · crown spread 12.7 m
Nearest town: Nelson
Location: Silver King Campus
Ownership: Institution/corp. · Selkirk College
Last measured: 11/8/2023
Site notes: The grand fir tree is located in a small, well-loved inland temperate rainforest in the back corner of the Selkirk College Silver King Campus. Neighbors walk their dogs through this forest, kids from the Silver King Childcare Centre go on outings in this forest (and have built a tree fort in it), and local mountain bikers have created a rudimentary pump track of berms, rollers, and jumps through it. There is very little understory due to the heavy human presence, but the cedar, hemlock, grand fir trees, and other trees appear to be thriving. There is an abundance of lichen hanging from tree boughs, and moss on the rocks. The grand fir we call Grandalf the Fir appears to have been part of a former art intallation, as there is faded red and green graffiti on his trunk, and the trunks of a pair of nearby cedars have been painted with the faces of ghoulish forest sprites. Grandalf has also been climbed, at least his lower section, as someone inserted a wooden seating platform in his boughs, approximately 5 metres off the ground. There is also evidence that someone used his lowest bough as a pull-up bar, as theres grippy athletic tape wrapped around it. Another of Grandalfs distinguishing features is a small forked trunk, at about 2 metres, which is dead and apparently died some time ago based on its short stature compared to Grandalfs soaring height.
Access notes: The grand fir is located in the forest adjacent to the Selkirk College Silver King Campus, on the campuss south side. From Nelson, BC, drive to the Selkirk College Silver King Campus and park in the lot. Walk to the back corner of the lot and enter the forest there. Look for a well-worn footpath leading up from the parking lot and into the trees. The grand fir is about a 1-minute walk.
